Cancer Therapy and Shared Decision-Making 
Considerations 

advance care planning, participate in shared decision-making, collaborate 
with palliative care specialists and teams as needed (especially for 
patients with complex care needs as indicated above), and ensure timely 
referral to hospice services. 

Patients who have months to years to live and a good performance status 
are likely to be interested in continuing cancer therapy to prolong survival 
and reduce cancer-related symptoms.172-175 Cancer therapy may be 
conventional evidence-based treatment as outlined in the NCCN 
disease-specific Guidelines (available at www.NCCN.org) or treatment in 
the context of a clinical trial. In some of the advanced-stage cancers, 
chemotherapy may be superior to best supportive care and may prolong 
survival.176,177 Palliative RT and/or interventional procedures also play an 
important role in the comprehensive care of patients with advanced 
cancer.178-184 To assess the risk of serious complications in patients with 
neutropenic fever, the Panel recommends referring to the NCCN 
Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-Related Infections 
and NCCN Guidelines for Hematopoietic Growth Factors (available at 
www.NCCN.org). 

The Panel divided patients into three groups to address the effect of life 
expectancy on the delivery of key palliative care interventions: 1) patients 
with months to years to live; 2) patients with weeks to months to live; and 
3) dying patients in their final days to weeks. Patients in their final hours of 
life are referred to as imminently dying and may require special 
interventions. The Panel recognizes the lack of precision in estimating life 
expectancy but believes that this delineation is useful for the delivery of 
appropriate palliative care interventions. The patient and family’s personal, 
spiritual and existential, cultural, and religious goals, values, and 
expectations may change throughout these timeframes. Optimal provision 
of palliative care requires ongoing reassessment and modification of 
strategies, as well as ongoing communication between the patient, family, 
caregiver(s), and health care team. 

Indicators that a patient’s prognosis is worsening include decreased 
performance status (ECOG score ≥3; KPS score ≤50), persistent 
hypercalcemia, central nervous system metastases, delirium, MBO, 
superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome, spinal cord compression, cachexia, 
malignant effusions, need for palliative stenting or venting gastronomy, 
potentially life-limiting disease, or other serious comorbid conditions. Many 
patients with stage IV cancers, especially those with metastatic lung 
cancer, pancreatic cancer, and glioblastoma multiforme, would benefit 
from palliative care beginning at diagnosis, because expected survival is 
limited.160,168-171 Palliative care interventions for managing specific 
symptoms and the benefits and burdens of anticancer therapy are 
discussed below as outlined in the algorithm. 

Furthermore, patients with advanced cancer who are not eligible for 
systemic chemotherapy may benefit from immunotherapy or molecular 
targeted therapies that may be effective for relieving symptoms, 
maintaining stable disease, and/or improving quality of life without the 
adverse events that may be associated with cytotoxic cancer 
therapies.185,186 Physicians, patients, and their families should discuss 
prognosis, intent and goals of therapy (curative or noncurative), range of 
choices, benefits and burdens of cancer therapy, implications of disease 
and/or treatment on their physical and cognitive function, and possible 
effects on quality of life. For management of fertility and intimacy 
concerns, please see the NCCN Guidelines for Survivorship (available at 
www.NCCN.org). In addition, the oncology team should discuss the 
possibility of disease progression or recurrence. For an approach to 
decision-making in older adults and geriatric screening tools, see the 

MS-14

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
NCCN Guidelines for Older Adult Oncology (available at 
www.NCCN.org). 

advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma.193 The Panel emphasizes the 
importance of initiating or continuing advance care planning conversations 
and systematically reviewing advance care plans to ensure ongoing 
accuracy as illness or the situation evolves. To avoid demeaning the value 
of end-of-life care, palliative care and/or hospice care should not be 
framed as “giving up,” but instead refocusing the care plan to achieve a 
better quality of life. It may be helpful to determine the patient and family’s 
prior experience(s) with end-of-life care. In addition, if appropriate, patients 
and families should be encouraged to complete any necessary legal 
documents. Clinicians, if appropriate, may assess and document the 
preferred location of death. Education and support related to care 
including referral to specialized palliative care services or hospice at the 
end of life should be offered. 

In general, patients with days to weeks to live (eg, dying patients) and 
comfort-oriented goals should discontinue all treatments not directly 
contributing to patient comfort. Intensive palliative care focusing on 
symptom management should be provided in addition to preparation for 
the dying process. Referral for hospice care should be placed, if not 
already done. Culturally/spiritually significant rituals/ceremonies important 
at the end of life may be considered upon patient request. 

Clinicians should provide primary palliative care to include both cancer 
treatments aligned with patient goals and priorities and disease-related 
symptom management. The appropriateness of palliative RT or 
interventional procedures should be assessed, and palliative procedures 
conducted should be in line with the goals of care. Cancer therapy should 
be in line with stated patient goals and priorities and be accompanied by 
appropriate prevention/management of side effects as well as palliative 
care. A longitudinal cohort study evaluated the impact of palliative 
chemotherapy on quality of life near death as a function of patient 
performance status. In patients with progressive metastatic cancer, 
palliative chemotherapy did not improve quality of life near death for those 
with moderate or poor performance status and worsened quality of life 
near death for those with initially good performance status.187 Studies have 
reported that, at times, cancer therapy may continue beyond what is 
evidence-based for patients with advanced or metastatic disease.80,188,189 
In some cases, nonpharmacologic and/or integrative interventions (eg, 
cognitive-behavioral, massage, and music or art therapy) may be 
considered. 

Advance Care Planning 

Patients with weeks to months to live should be provided with guidance 
regarding the anticipated course of the disease. Physicians should 
reassess prognostic awareness and goals of therapy. As functional status 
worsens, these patients may become more concerned about the side 
effects of cancer-directed treatment and consider focusing their care on 
maintaining quality of life. The option of discontinuing cancer treatment 
aligned with goals of care and initiating goal-directed supportive care 
should be discussed.186,187,190-192 A retrospective, single-center, 
observational study suggests that palliative care may be associated with 
longer survival after chemotherapy discontinuation in patients with 

The oncology team should assess and cultivate prognostic awareness and 
integrate discussions of personal values and preferences for current and 
future care while patients have a life expectancy of months to years. The 
patient’s decision-making capacity should also be assessed, and a 
surrogate decision-maker should be identified. Several studies have 
shown that these discussions frequently happen too late in the trajectory 
of disease, often during acute hospital care and often with health 
professionals other than the primary oncologist.194-196 Earlier integration of 
advance care planning discussions has been associated with less 

MS-15

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
across care settings. Documentation of surrogate decision maker is best 
practice. The team should also confirm the patient’s values and decisions 
in light of changes in status. 

aggressive care and increased use of hospice,197,198 while less aggressive 
care has been associated with an improved quality of life.199 Studies 
suggest that most patients with cancer would prefer to die at home,200,201 
but lack of timely advance care planning can render this impossible. 

A randomized controlled trial of a structured intervention to facilitate 
end-of-life discussions (consisting of an informational pamphlet and 
provider discussion) led to earlier designation of do-not-resuscitate orders 
and decreased the likelihood of patients dying in the hospital.202 In 
addition, a study showed that electronic prompts and email reminders to 
doctors could increase documentation rates of code status in patients with 
advanced lung cancer.203 A 2015 systematic review summarizes the 
evidence base from randomized trials of interventions designed to 
promote shared decision-making and advance care planning in patients 
with serious illness.204 

Advance care planning should identify personal values, goals, 
expectations, and priorities and assess their congruence with those of the 
family/caregiver/health care team. Formal documents including advance 
directives, living wills, medical powers of attorney, and health care proxy 
should be completed. Any other documents delineating specific limitations 
regarding life-sustaining treatments (eg, CPR, mechanical ventilation, 
artificial nutrition/hydration), as well as an open discussion about palliative 
care options such as hospice should be completed as appropriate. A 
patient’s values and preferences and any decisions should be 
documented in the medical record, including MOLST or POLST (Medical 
Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment or Physician Orders for 
Life-Sustaining Treatment) if completed.205 

Clinicians, if appropriate, may assess and document the preferred location 
of death. Most patients with cancer would prefer to spend their remaining 
time at home,200,201 but sometimes their care needs are too great to be 
feasible in the home. Some patients request to receive end-of-life care in a 
skilled nursing facility or an in-patient hospice facility.201,206 A prospective 
study showed that patients dying in an ICU had higher levels of physical 
and emotional distress compared with patients dying at home or in 
hospice. Additionally, caregivers of these patients had a greater incidence 
of prolonged grief disorder.207 Providing palliative care services has been 
shown to decrease deaths in ICUs.206 A retrospective cohort study showed 
that patients who wanted to be at home at the end of life were more likely 
to do so if they had daily hospice visits, if they were married, if they had 
advance directives, if they did not have moderate or severe pain, or if they 
had good performance status.201 A second retrospective study suggested 
that referral to specialist palliative care at a greater interval of time prior to 
death increased the likelihood of patients dying at home or in hospice 
rather than in the hospital.208 If advance care plans have not been 
completed, the oncology team should explore the patient’s reluctance to 
engage in advance care planning and refer to palliative care if needed. 
Referral to a specialized palliative care service can be considered if the 
patient is having difficulty engaging in discussion of advance care planning 
to explore their fears and worries about illness. Additional referrals to a 
chaplain/spiritual care counselor and to a mental health clinician can be 
considered to explore well-being. Additional information on assessment 
and management of psychosocial and emotional distress can be found in 
the NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management (available at 
www.NCCN.org). Anxiety and depression could result in lesser 
engagement with advance care planning since they are commonly 

When the patient’s life expectancy is reduced to weeks to months, the 
oncology team should actively facilitate the completion of appropriate 
advance directives and ensure their availability in all care settings. 
MOLST/POLST should be documented and accessible to all providers 

MS-16

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
Pain 

elevated among patients with advanced cancers. Practical strategies and 
sample scripts for oncology care providers are provided to reduce the 
effects of anxiety and depression in these contexts.209 Clinicians should 
also consider offering anticipatory guidance as part of interventional 
strategy. 

See the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain (available at 
www.NCCN.org) for specific recommendations for pain management, 
including opioid principles, prescribing, titration, maintenance, and 
safety. Clinicians should be aware of state and local regulations regarding 
opioid prescriptions. 

In patients with a life expectancy of days to weeks, the patient’s decision 
regarding CPR and other life-sustaining treatments should be clarified and 
confirmed. Education about the benefits and limitations of CPR should be 
provided, and documentation of the resuscitation orders including in 
POLST/MOLST as per patient/family/caregiver preferences should be 
completed as appropriate. Providers should facilitate continued 
involvement of the primary care physician and primary oncology team. The 
desire for organ donation and/or autopsy should also be explored with the 
patient. The oncology team should ensure that the care provided adheres 
to the patient’s advance care plan. Education and support related to care 
at the end of life should be offered. 

Symptom Management 

In addition, it is also important to be aware of several general 
considerations when addressing pain symptoms near the end of life. It is 
important to educate the patient/family/caregiver(s) about the patient’s 
condition, prognosis, and the importance of pain control at the end of life. 
Optimizing psychosocial and spiritual support for the 
patient/family/caregiver(s) and customizing the education and support to 
the patient and family/caregiver(s) need to be considered. Integrative 
interventions may be considered for patients with life expectancies of 
days to weeks; see the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain 
(available at www.NCCN.org). If feasible and desired, pain management 
should be balanced against reduced level of consciousness. Routes of 
pain medication delivery may need to be modified as a patient 
approaches the end of life applying equianalgesic dose conversions. It is 
also important to recognize and treat opioid-induced neurotoxicity, 
including myoclonus and hyperalgesia. Opioid rotation can be 
considered if needed. Single-fraction palliative RT may be used to 
address pain associated with bone metastases.183,184,214,215 Study data 
suggest that 40% of patients (122/298) who received a single 8 Gy RT 
dose for painful bone metastases experienced pain reduction and 
improved quality of life within 10 days and may be recommended for 
patients with a life expectancy of multiple weeks.215 216-222 Clinicians 
should maintain ongoing shared decision-making to balance the burdens 
and benefits that come with palliative RT.223,224 

With regard to symptoms, the management of pain, dyspnea, 
anorexia/cachexia, nausea and vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, MBO, 
fatigue, delirium, and psychological distress are fundamental210-212 and are 
discussed in detail below. Symptoms should be comprehensively 
assessed in all patients. In patients who are non-communicative, symptom 
intensity may be assessed using physical signs. Education should be 
provided to the patient/family/caregiver(s) on the patient’s condition and 
the risk/benefit of treatment options. In addition to education, psychosocial 
and emotional support for the patient/family/caregiver(s) is also an 
important part of symptom management. Digital apps can be utilized as a 
way of assessing or monitoring symptoms.213 As a general principle, 
if/when appropriate, providers should try to use palliative interventions that 
may address multiple symptoms. 

MS-17

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
Dyspnea 

benzodiazepines on dyspnea in patients with advanced cancer is small, 
and the addition of benzodiazepines to opioids can increase the risk of 
respiratory depression. In patients towards the end of life, a 
benzodiazepine can be considered, particularly when dyspnea is 
associated with anxiety and when opioids and other non-pharmacologic 
measures have not controlled dyspnea.230,240 If fluid overload is thought to 
be a contributing factor for dyspnea, consider decreasing fluids and/or low-
dose diuretics, based on the clinical situation. 

Opioids, in low doses, at the lowest effective dose with titration as 
appropriate to the lowest effective dose, can be used to treat dyspnea that 
is resistant to other therapies. Low-dose opioid can be initiated in the 
opioid-naïve patient.241-246 For patients receiving chronic opioids, the Panel 
recommends consideration of a 25% dose increase to treat symptomatic 
dyspnea. Morphine should be avoided in patients with known renal 
compromise. For additional information on opioid medications and opioid 
titration, please see the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain 
(available at www.NCCN.org). 

Dyspnea is one of the most common symptoms in patients with advanced 
lung cancer.225 The American Thoracic Society consensus statement 
defines dyspnea as “a subjective experience of breathing discomfort that 
consists of qualitatively distinct sensations that vary in intensity.”226 
Potentially reversible underlying causes or comorbid conditions should be 
treated using chemotherapy or RT or other interventional strategies as 
appropriate. If dyspnea is immunotherapy-induced, refer to the NCCN 
Guidelines for Management of CAR T-Cell and Lymphocyte Engager-
Related Toxicities and the NCCN Guidelines for Management of Immune 
Checkpoint Inhibitor-Related Toxicities (available at www.NCCN.org); 
Therapeutic procedures for cardiac, pleural, or abdominal fluid227-229; 
bronchoscopic therapy; or bronchodilators, diuretics, steroids, antibiotics, 
transfusions, or anticoagulants are recommended for prevention of 
pulmonary emboli. Oxygen therapy for symptomatic hypoxia is also 
recommended. Both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic interventions 
have been investigated in the management of dyspnea. While there are 
little definitive data evaluating the effectiveness of dyspnea 
interventions,230,231 the Panel members agree that there are sufficient data 
to make treatment recommendations.228,232 

Scopolamine, atropine, hyoscyamine, and glycopyrrolate are options to 
reduce excessive secretions associated with dyspnea, particularly if at the 
end of life.247-251 Glycopyrrolate does not effectively cross the blood–brain 
barrier and is less likely than the other drug options to cause delirium, but 
this agent can still produce anticholinergic side effects.252-254 Scopolamine 
can be administered transdermally. Physicians should be aware that the 
onset of benefit for transdermal scopolamine patches is about 12 hours;255 
thus, they may not be an appropriate choice for imminently dying patients. 

The Panel recommends first considering non-pharmacologic interventions 
including the use of handheld fans directed at the face,233,234 cooler 
temperatures, stress management, relaxation therapy, and physical 
comfort measures. A randomized controlled trial examined the effects of 
room air versus palliative oxygen delivered via nasal cannula in patients 
with refractory dyspnea. Dyspnea scores were no different among patients 
receiving palliative oxygen versus room air, encouraging the use of less 
burdensome interventions after brief assessment of the effect of oxygen 
therapy on the individual patient.235 If nonpharmacologic measures do not 
provide desired relief, pharmacologic interventions may be considered 
including opioids.228,230,231,236-239 The reported beneficial effect of 

High-flow nasal oxygen and noninvasive mechanical ventilation are 
generally not available outside of the acute care setting but may provide 
temporary improvements in hypoxemia and dyspnea. In a feasibility study 
of 200 patients with solid tumors randomized to receive either noninvasive 
positive-pressure ventilation (bilevel positive airway pressure, BiPAP) or 

MS-18

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
conventional oxygen therapy, patients in the ventilation group had greater 
improvements in dyspnea symptoms and required lower doses of opiates 
than patients in the oxygen group.256 A smaller phase II randomized trial 
comparing high-flow oxygen to BiPAP for persistent dyspnea in patients 
with advanced cancer revealed no significant differences between the two 
approaches.257 Palliative RT can be considered in appropriate situations, 
such as for patients with symptomatic SVC syndrome or those who have 
respiratory obstruction by tumor mass.178,258,259 Noninvasive positive-
pressure ventilation support (eg, continuous positive airway pressure 
[CPAP], BiPAP) is recommended if clinically indicated for a severe, 
potentially reversible condition if in line with a patient’s goals of care. 

needed and dosed as per clinical scenario. A symptom known as the 
“death rattle” may present in patients with a life expectancy of days to 
weeks stemming from the loss of the ability to swallow and/or clear oral 
secretions resulting in a rattling or gurgling noise. The sounds of this 
symptom may distress the family/caregiver(s) since a fear of the patient 
choking without conscious control may be unsettling.261 Patients may 
require gentle suction of the oral pharynx, avoiding deep suctioning to help 
provide relief from secretions in the upper and lower respiratory tracts.262 
Further, positioning the patient in a different position to facilitate drainage 
as well as counselling the family/caregiver(s) regarding these symptoms 
may help relieve the patient and aid in easing the immediate concerns of 
the family/caregiver(s).263-265 

Anorexia/Cachexia 

Cachexia, characterized by physical wasting with loss of both skeletal and 
visceral muscle mass, is a common condition among patients with 
cancer.266,267 Many patients with cancer lose the desire to eat (anorexia), 
which contributes to cachexia. Cachexia can also occur independently 
from anorexia, as proinflammatory cytokines and tumor-derived factors 
directly lead to muscle proteolysis.266,267 Cachexia leads to asthenia 
(weakness), hypoalbuminemia, emaciation, immune system impairment, 
metabolic dysfunction, and autonomic failure. Cancer-related cachexia has 
also been associated with disease progression despite cancer treatment, 
increased treatment toxicity, delayed treatment initiation, early treatment 
termination, shorter survival, and psychosocial distress.266-268 A study that 
examined cancer cachexia in a cohort of 1473 patients across all weight 
ranges showed that muscle depletion conveys a similarly poor prognosis 
as involuntary weight loss, regardless of body mass index.269 

Initial steps include evaluating the rate and severity of weight loss and 
associated symptoms and educating the patient/family/caregiver(s) on the 
patient’s condition and discussing the risk/benefit of available treatment 

When caring for actively dying patients, providers should discuss the 
reversibility of respiratory failure and treatment options, and provide 
anticipatory guidance for patient/family/caregiver(s) about dying of 
respiratory failure.260 The Panel recommends first considering 
nonpharmacologic therapies, including educational, psychosocial-spiritual, 
and emotional supportive measures. Other interventions to maintain cooler 
temperatures (including fans) should be considered. If nonpharmacologic 
measures do not provide desired relief, pharmacologic therapies may be 
considered as discussed above, including oxygen supplementation (if 
hypoxia present and/or subjective relief is reported); a trial of low-dose 
opioids with close monitoring of adverse events and appropriate dose 
titration in patients who are opioid tolerant; and/or benzodiazepines, when 
opioids and other non-pharmacologic measures have not controlled 
dyspnea. Interventions such as a high-flow nasal cannula may be 
considered, if consistent with the patient’s goals and values. However, as 
life expectancy decreases, the role of mechanical ventilation and oxygen 
diminishes, and the role of other non-pharmacologic therapies and 
pharmacologic interventions increases. If fluid overload is a contributing 
factor, there should be consideration of decreasing enteral and parenteral 
fluids and/or addition of low-dose diuretics (such as furosemide) given as

pages.text:
rates of edema, thrombosis, and death among patients using the drug. 
When compared to other drugs, such as corticosteroids, there was no 
improvement in quality of life or appetite. 

options. Clinicians should address conditions or symptoms that interfere 
with food intake. Oral health symptoms (eg, dysgeusia, xerostomia, 
dental/jaw issues, mucositis, oropharyngeal candidiasis),270-272 early 
satiety, intractable hiccups, psychiatric symptoms (eg, depression, anxiety, 
eating disorders/distorted body image), gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, 
nausea/vomiting, constipation), pain, fatigue, and pancreatic exocrine 
enzyme insufficiency, among others, and psychiatric evaluation may be 
considered if the patient has a history of an eating disorder, depression, or 
phobia/anxiety related to swallowing/eating challenges. Treatment may 
include modifying medications or the relief of symptoms that interfere with 
food intake (eg, pain, constipation, nausea/vomiting), as well as 
metoclopramide for early satiety due to gut dysmotility.228,232,273 Endocrine 
abnormalities such as thyroid dysfunction should be taken into account in 
the assessment since this may contribute to malnutrition. The Panel 
recommends avoiding metoclopramide in the setting of complete bowel 
obstruction. A swallowing evaluation may also be considered. It is 
important to assess complexities related to social determinants of health. 
High protein, high nutrition foods may be encouraged for the patient to 
help with nutritional status. 

Appetite stimulants may be helpful (eg, dexamethasone, olanzapine) if 
increased appetite is an important aspect of quality of life.274-278 Systematic 
reviews and meta-analyses of megestrol acetate demonstrate improved 
appetite and slight improvements in weight gain when using this drug to 
treat anorexia/cachexia in patients with cancer.275,279 While one quarter of 
patients treated with megestrol acetate may have increased appetite and 1 
in 12 may improve their weight, clinicians should be mindful of the 
increased risks of thromboembolic phenomena and death.275 

A Cochrane review published in 2013275 that reviewed 35 clinical trials that 
showed some improvement in weight gain, quality of life, and appetite in 
patients with cancer when compared to placebo, highlighted the higher 

Although cannabinoid-based interventions (eg, dronabinol, cannabis 
[colloquially known as marijuana]) have some demonstrated efficacy for 
treating chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and AIDS-related 
anorexia, the data to support cannabinoid-based interventions for treating 
anorexia/cachexia in patients with cancer are very limited, in part due to 
legal constraints within this field of research.275,280,281 A randomized clinical 
trial of cannabis extract and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol in patients with 
cancer-related anorexia-cachexia syndrome did not demonstrate a benefit 
of these agents over placebo on appetite and quality of life.282 Another 
randomized trial comparing megestrol acetate to dronabinol in treating 
cancer-associated anorexia revealed megestrol acetate to be superior for 
promoting weight gain (75% vs. 49% of patients) and appetite (11% vs. 
3%) in patients with advanced cancer.283 However, to a lesser extent, 
dronabinol did improve appetite and weight gain in some study patients. 
Ultimately, for some patients with cancer-related anorexia, cannabinoids 
could be helpful. However, it is important to note that cannabinoid 
administration in patients who are older may induce delirium, and 
providers should be aware of the local state rules and regulations 
regarding medicinal cannabinoid use. On a narrative review on the use of 
cannabinoids in palliating cancer-related symptoms, Hatsfield et al 
concluded that cannabinoid products should not be routinely 
recommended for cancer supportive care based on conflicting evidence.284 
The Panel noted that the quality of evidence for the routine use of 
megestrol acetate or cannabinoids in patients with cancer cachexia is 
lacking, and clinicians must assess if the benefits of using pharmacologic 
therapy outweigh the risks. The Panel highlighted that clinicians may 
choose not to prescribe pharmacologic intervention for cancer cachexia 
and treatment. If they do choose to use pharmacologic interventions,

pages.text:
clinicians should counsel patients about the risks, benefits, and options for 
cachexia treatment and reassess on an ongoing basis with consideration 
of stopping therapy if ineffective.280,282-284 

aspects of withdrawal of nutritional support. Nutritional consultation may 
be considered. Eating for pleasure may also be considered but should not 
be forced upon patients with no hunger or thirst. Enrolling in a clinical trial 
with a novel cachexia medication, such as growth differentiation factor 15 
(GDF-15) inhibitor ponsegromab (which is currently under investigation for 
use in patients with cancer cachexia), may be considered in certain 
circumstances for eligible patients.295 

Nausea and Vomiting 

Although some studies show nutritional interventions to be ineffective,285 
consultation with a registered dietitian should be considered, because 
calorie-dense, high-protein supplementation has demonstrated some 
efficacy for weight stabilization.228,266,286-288 A meta-analysis found that 
while nutritional intervention does not significantly affect weight gain or 
energy intake, it can improve some aspects of quality of life, including 
emotional functioning, dyspnea, and hunger.289 Nutritional support, 
including enteral and parenteral feeding as appropriate, should also be 
considered when the disease or treatment affects the ability to eat and/or 
absorb nutrients and the patient’s life expectancy is months to years.290 

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting has a major impact on a 
patient’s quality of life.296 Nausea and vomiting induced by chemotherapy 
or RT should be managed as outlined in the NCCN Guidelines for 
Antiemesis (available at www.NCCN.org). Patients who are looking for 
alternative treatment options for nausea and vomiting related to 
chemotherapy or RT may consider acupressure.297 Patients can also 
experience nausea and vomiting unrelated to chemotherapy and radiation, 
resulting from gastrointestinal obstruction, bowel obstruction, constipation, 
opioid use, or hypercalcemia.298 These causes should be identified and 
treated. Palliative RT and corticosteroids should be considered for nausea 
and vomiting related to brain metastases.178,299,300 Proton pump inhibitors 
and histamine-2 (H2) receptor antagonists can be used to manage 
gastritis or gastroesophageal reflux. Gastrointestinal obstruction may 
benefit from treatment with corticosteroids, a proton pump inhibitor, and 
metoclopramide. However, for patients with complete gastric outlet 
obstruction, metoclopramide should be avoided; alternative treatment 
options include endoscopic stenting or insertion of a decompressing 
nasogastric or gastrostomy tube. Many medications (including 
non-prescribed supplements and herbs) can also cause nausea and 
vomiting. Blood levels should be checked for possible culprits, such as 
digoxin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and tricyclic antidepressants.301,302 
Also, patients should be screened for excess use of cannabis for possible 

The goals and intensity of nutritional support change as life expectancy is 
reduced to days to weeks. Absence of hunger and thirst is normal in the 
dying patient, and nutritional support may not reverse weight loss in 
patients with advanced cancer. Education and emotional support should 
be provided regarding the natural history of the disease, as artificial 
nutrition and hydration may increase the risk of fluid overload, aspiration, 
infection, and hastened death. Overly aggressive enteral or parenteral 
nutrition therapies can actually increase the suffering of dying patients, 
and therefore, discontinuing previously initiated enteral or parenteral 
nutrition near the end of life is appropriate, is ethically permissible, and 
may improve some symptoms.290-293 A randomized controlled trial of 
patients with cancer enrolled in hospice found that parenteral hydration 
had no effect on dehydration symptoms such as fatigue and hallucination, 
nor any effect on quality of life or survival.294 Therefore, instead of artificial 
hydration and nutrition, palliative care in the final weeks of life focuses on 
treating dry mouth and thirst, and providing education and emotional 
support to the patient, family, and caregiver(s) regarding the emotional 

MS-21

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
cannabis-associated hyperemesis syndrome, and counseled regarding 
cessation if indicated. 

provided as needed, scheduled, or continuously. Subcutaneous or 
parenteral administration of antiemetic agents can also be used as an 
alternative. An around-the-clock dosing schedule may provide the most 
consistent benefit to the patient. Continuous IV or subcutaneous infusions 
of different antiemetics may be necessary for the management of 
intractable nausea and vomiting. Alternating timing of agents can be 
considered to optimize nausea and vomiting control. 

Constipation 

Non-specific nausea and vomiting are often managed with dopamine– or 
5-HT3 (5-hydroxytryptamine 3)–receptor antagonists (eg, 
prochlorperazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide, olanzapine, ondansetron). 
However, experts have debated the quality and strength of the evidence to 
support specific agents in the management of nonspecific nausea and 
vomiting in palliative care.303,304 A systematic review assessed the level of 
evidence for antiemesis unrelated to chemotherapy, concluding that 
antiemetic recommendations have moderate to weak evidence at best.304 
There is an emerging body of evidence for use of olanzapine in non-
specific nausea and vomiting.305-307 For anxiety-related nausea (including 
anticipatory nausea), the addition of benzodiazepines can be considered. 
If a vertiginous component to nausea and vomiting exists, 
anticholinergic/antihistamine agents may be appropriate. 
Non-pharmacologic therapies such as acupuncture, hypnosis, and 
cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also be considered.308-310 When 
patients experience dehydration, uremia, or hypercalcemia, the Panel 
recommends appropriate treatment as indicated. 

Constipation occurs in approximately 60% of patients with advanced 
cancer and most patients treated with opioids.324,325 Although several drugs 
including antacids, anticholinergic drugs (antidepressants, 
antispasmodics, phenothiazines, and haloperidol), and antiemetics are 
known to cause constipation,326 opioid analgesics are most commonly 
associated with constipation. In addition to physical discomfort, 
constipation in patients with advanced cancer can cause psychological 
distress and anxiety regarding continued opioid use.327 Opioid-induced 
constipation (OIC) should be anticipated and treated prophylactically with 
a stimulant laxative to achieve a goal of one non-forced bowel movement 
every 1 to 2 days and add an osmotic laxative if patient can tolerate the 
liquid volume.328 Increasing fluid intake and physical activity should also be 
encouraged, when appropriate. 

For persistent nausea and vomiting, the Panel recommends titrating 
dopamine receptor antagonists to maximum benefit and tolerance.311-315 In 
the setting of continued nausea and vomiting, consider additional drug 
classes with potential antiemetic properties: corticosteroids,316-318 5-HT3 
receptor antagonists,319-321 anticholinergic agents and/or antihistamines,317 
or oral cannabinoids.322,323 The appropriate route and frequency of 
administration should be considered; the Panel recommends prescribing 
oral, sublingual, or rectal agent as appropriate and titrating to maximum 
benefit. Opioid rotation can also be considered for patients taking opioid 
medications that may be causing or exacerbating nausea and vomiting. 
For persistent/refractory nausea and vomiting, parenteral infusions can be 

Preventive measures for constipation include optimizing food intake and 
physical activity as appropriate, as well as administering prophylactic 
medications like stimulant laxatives and osmotic laxatives. Increasing 
laxative doses with the goal of one non-forced bowel movement every 1 to 
2 days is recommended. Stimulant laxatives can be titrated as tolerated in 
patients with persistent constipation. If constipation is present, the cause 
and severity should be assessed. Impaction, obstruction, and other 
treatable causes, such as hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, hypothyroidism, 
and diabetes mellitus, and side effects of immunotherapy should be 

MS-22

pages.text:
Diarrhea 

In patients with cancer, diarrhea can be caused by a number of potential 
factors, including cancer treatment-related side effects, infection, antibiotic 
use, dietary changes, or fecal impaction.336 Diarrhea is a common side 
effect of various chemotherapeutics (eg, fluorouracil and irinotecan), as 
well as tyrosine kinase inhibitors and certain biologic agents (eg, 
ipilimumab, cetuximab, panitumumab).337-340 Abdominal and pelvic RT 
(alone or as part of chemoradiation regimens) can also induce 
gastrointestinal toxicity resulting in diarrhea.338,339 

The National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse 
Events (CTCAE) are typically used for measuring diarrhea in this patient 
population.336 The Panel recommends that patients be screened and 
assessed to determine the severity (grade) and cause of diarrhea. 
Providers should provide immediate intervention for dehydration based on 
grade and tailor treatment to potential causes. 

identified and treated. Providers should discontinue any nonessential 
constipating medications. If impaction is observed, glycerin suppositories 
(with or without mineral oil retention enema) may be administered or 
manual disimpaction may be performed following pre-medication with an 
analgesic and/or anxiolytic. Suppositories and enemas should be used 
with caution in patients receiving chemotherapy due to the increased risk 
of the rectal route of administration in the setting of cytopenia. While there 
is limited evidence regarding the best initial bowel regimen in patients with 
cancer,329 one small study compared the use of senna alone versus a 
senna-docusate combination. The results suggested that the addition of 
the stool softener docusate was not necessary.330 If constipation persists, 
adding other laxatives may be considered, such as rectal bisacodyl once 
daily or oral polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium hydroxide, or 
magnesium citrate.329 Magnesium-containing products should be avoided 
in patients with renal failure. If gastroparesis is suspected, the addition of a 
prokinetic agent, such as metoclopramide, may be considered. 

For patients who have grade 1 (mild) or 2 (moderate) diarrhea, 
recommendations include hydration and electrolyte replacement (oral or IV 
fluids as appropriate) and antidiarrheal medications (eg, loperamide). If 
diarrhea is thought to be chemotherapy-related, dose reduction or 
discontinuation of therapy may be appropriate. For diarrhea due to irritable 
bowel syndrome (IBS), utilize cognitive behavioral interventions 
complementary to medication intervention.341 

Peripherally acting µ-opioid receptor antagonists (PAMORAs) may help to 
relieve resistant OIC while maintaining pain management.331 Studies have 
shown that methylnaltrexone provided effective relief of OIC while 
preserving opioid-mediated analgesia.332,333 Naloxegol, a similar 
PAMORA, has also been studied for treating OIC in patients receiving 
chronic opioids for noncancer pain.334,335 Based on these results, 
methylnaltrexone every other day (no more than once a day) can be 
considered for patients experiencing OIC that has not responded to at 
least two different classes of standard laxative therapy. Methylnaltrexone 
should not be used in patients with postoperative ileus or mechanical 
bowel obstruction. If oral therapy is not effective, enemas may be 
considered as needed. The presence of renal failure in patients with OIC 
warrants caution when using sodium phosphate enemas. 

For grade 2 diarrhea, anticholinergic agents such as hyoscyamine or 
atropine can be considered in addition to the interventions recommended 
for grade 1. Infection-induced diarrhea should be treated with the 
appropriate antibiotic. Immunotherapy-related diarrhea can be treated with 
corticosteroids, infliximab, and/or probiotics (see the NCCN Guidelines for 
Management of CAR T-Cell and Lymphocyte Engager-Related Toxicities 
and the NCCN Guidelines for Management of Immune Checkpoint

and re-obstruction.342 Although surgery is the primary treatment for 
malignant obstruction, some patients with advanced disease or patients in 
generally poor condition are unfit for surgery and require alternative 
treatment to relieve distressing symptoms. Risk factors for poor surgical 
outcome include ascites, carcinomatosis, palpable intra-abdominal 
masses, multifocal bowel obstructions, previous abdominal radiation, 
advanced disease, and poor overall clinical status.343 In these patients, 
medical management can include pharmacologic measures, parenteral 
fluids, endoscopic management, and enteral tube drainage (silicone tubing 
may offer superior comfort over vinyl). 

Inhibitor-Related Toxicities [available at www.NCCN.org]). In these 
instances, screening for Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), human 
immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and comorbid infections such as ova and 
parasites should be considered. Antibiotics and probiotics should be used 
in cases where C. diff infections are involved with diarrhea. IV fluids are 
recommended if patients are unable to tolerate oral fluids. Patients with 
grade 3 or 4 (severe) diarrhea should receive inpatient treatment 
(intensive care for Grade 4 diarrhea) if consistent with patient goals. In 
addition to fluid replacement, antidiarrheal therapy, and anticholinergics, 
somatostatin analogs (eg, octreotide) can also be considered. For diarrhea 
due to graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), diet alterations including IV 
nutrition and steroids may be necessary. Additionally, tinctures of opium 
may be considered for patients with grade 3 or 4 diarrhea. 

For patients with days to weeks of estimated life expectancy, the above 
interventions can be considered if consistent with the patient’s goals of 
care. At-home IV hydration may be considered in addition to scopolamine 
or hyoscyamine. If diarrhea persists, consider octreotide or glycopyrrolate. 

Malignant Bowel Obstruction 

Initial steps should include evaluating the severity and cause(s) of bowel 
obstruction and educating the patient, family, and caregiver(s) on the 
patient’s condition and available treatment options. Underlying causes that 
are potentially reversible as well as malignant causes should be identified 
and treated. MBOs are usually diagnosed clinically and confirmed with 
radiography. The choice of intervention should be guided by the goals of 
treatment, considering prognosis and relative invasiveness of the 
intervention proposed. 

Pharmacologic management of MBO can be separated into two groups of 
patients: those for whom the goal is to maintain gut function and those for 
whom gut function is no longer possible. When the goal is maintaining gut 
function, patients can be treated with opioids, antiemetics, and 
corticosteroids, alone or in combination. When gut function is no longer 
considered possible, pharmacologic options also include somatostatin 
analogs (eg, octreotide) and/or anticholinergics.344-348 If octreotide is 
helpful and the patient has a life expectancy of at least 1 month, it may be 
beneficial to consider a depot form of octreotide once an optimal dose is 
established. Antiemetics that increase gastrointestinal mobility such as 
metoclopramide should not be used in patients with complete obstruction 
but may be beneficial when obstruction is partial. Use of octreotide is 
recommended early in the diagnosis because of its efficacy and 
tolerability.349,350 Despite positive findings from several smaller randomized 
trials, a phase III trial of octreotide in 87 patients with MBO did not 
demonstrate a significant effect of this drug on days free of vomiting; 
however, in the octreotide group, multivariate analysis did suggest a 
reduced number of vomiting episodes during the study period.351 If 
steroids are used, discontinue them if ineffective after 3 to 5 days. 

For patients with months to years to live, surgery (eg, resection, bypass, 
diverting ostomy) following CT scan is the primary treatment option. While 
surgery can lead to improvements in quality of life, surgical risks should be

pages.text:
A venting gastrostomy tube (inserted by interventional radiology, 
endoscopy, or surgery) or an endoscopically placed stent can also palliate 
symptoms of MBO.352-356 

Primary sleep disorders, such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), restless 
legs syndrome, and periodic limb movement disorder, should be 
considered for evaluation with a sleep study (if prognosis allows) and 
treated with nocturnal CPAP or BiPAP.365 Restless legs syndrome, if 
present, can be treated with ropinirole, pramipexole, pregabalin, 
gabapentin (for chronic symptoms), or carbidopa-levodopa and 
clonazepam (for intermittent symptoms).366-374 Dopamine agonists (eg, 
ropinirole and pramipexole) should be avoided with concurrent usage of 
dopamine antagonists (eg, haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine). Worries 
and anxiety regarding cancer-related stressors should be explored, and 
other factors that contribute to sleep/wake disturbances should be treated, 
including pain, depression, anxiety, delirium, and nausea. 

Since cancer treatments complicate morbidities such as malnutrition by 
potentially adding digestive disorders, total parenteral nutrition (TPN) can 
be considered in patients with a life expectancy of months to years when 
aligned with patient-specific goals for maintaining quality of life and after 
consideration of the risks and benefits.357 Complications of TPN that arise 
that should be considered before starting include infections and 
thromboses since indwelling lines and catheters represent potential means 
of complications.358 TPN may be considered in these select circumstances 
and with ongoing assessment of patient goals; however, TPN is not 
generally recommended at the end of life.168,169 Additionally, bowel rest 
should be considered as appropriate in order to allow the digestive system 
to recover. 

Sleep/Wake Disturbances Including Insomnia and Sedation 

Patients with cancer often suffer from insomnia or daytime sedation.336,359-

CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is a preferred strategy of first-line therapy over 
pharmacologic intervention. The clinical practice guidelines for the use of 
behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in 
adults from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM)232,362,375-379 
recommend that clinicians use multicomponent CBT-I for the treatment of 
chronic insomnia disorder in adults.375 A stepped care CBT-I with patients 
with less severe insomnia first receiving a web-based CBT-I was not 
inferior to those receiving face to face CBT-I. A stepped web-based 
intervention is a valuable approach to making this treatment more widely 
accessible to patients with cancer. However, this study excluded patients 
with a prognosis of <1 year, so the applicability in the palliative cancer 
population may be unclear.380 

362 In a study of 442 patients with advanced cancer, 330 (75%) patients 
were assessed as having baseline sleep disturbance as assessed by the 
Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) sleep item.363 For 
clinicians who wish to screen for insomnia, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale 
(ESS) is recommended.362,364 However, most clinicians involved in the 
psychosocial care of cancer survivors do not screen for insomnia, and no 
high-quality studies demonstrate that routine screening in patients with 
cancer for insomnia improves outcomes. The clinician should inquire 
about the patient’s desire to have insomnia and sedation treated. The type 
of severity of sleep/wake disturbance should first be evaluated, including 
daytime impairments and co-sleeper observations. 

A consultation to a physiatrist for a tailored exercise therapy program is 
also an appropriate intervention. Acupuncture has been shown to be 
effective for cancer-related insomnia.381 For more interventions for sleep 
disorders, see the NCCN Guidelines for Survivorship (available at 
www.NCCN.org).

appropriately.385 Delirium may present as either a hypoactive or a 
hyperactive subtype.386 Studies have suggested that hypoactive delirium 
was the most prevalent subtype in patients receiving palliative care and 
that this condition is often underdiagnosed due to its presentation.387,388 
Delirium-inducing medications (eg, steroids, anticholinergics, 
benzodiazepines) should be reduced or eliminated as much as possible.389 
Non-pharmacologic interventions (eg, optimization of sleep-wake cycle, 
addressing sensory impairment, providing glasses/hearing aids, and 
consideration of the role of exercise and activity including therapist-
supervised mobility activity) should be maximized before pharmacologic 
interventions are used for both patients with delirium and those at high risk 
for delirium. Caregivers should be supported in caring for their loved one 
and coping with this distressing condition. 

Screening for underlying reversible causes such as hypoxia, metabolic 
conditions, dehydration, unrelieved pain, bowel obstruction/obstipation, 
infections, brain metastases, and urinary retention may be addressed 
individually if necessary. Medications of substance effect or withdrawal 
(eg, benzodiazepines, opioids, anticholinergics, non-prescribed 
substances) should also be considered as part of the screening process 
for patients with suspected delirium. 

For isolated sleep-onset insomnia, consider pharmacologic management 
options that include melatonin; low-dose doxepin (with caution in older 
adults); trazodone; mirtazapine; dual orexin receptor antagonists 
(DORAs) such as daridorexant, lemborexant, and suvorexant; selective 
melatonin receptor agonist ramelteon; and benzodiazepine receptor 
agonists (BZRAs) such as zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon. Caution 
needs to be exercised when using BZRA in patients who are older, frail, 
have cognitive impairment, or are taking opioid medications. For sleep 
maintenance, DORAs and doxepin can be considered. For refractory 
insomnia, pharmacologic management options include antipsychotic 
medications such as chlorpromazine, quetiapine, and olanzapine; 
melatonin or the melatonin-receptor agonist ramelteon; and sedating 
antidepressants such as trazodone and mirtazapine.382 The Panel 
suggests that mirtazapine may be especially effective in patients with 
concurrent depression and anorexia. Benzodiazepines should be avoided, 
particularly among patients who are older, on opioid medications, and with 
cognitive impairment, because these agents have been shown to cause 
decreased cognitive performance.383 Similar caution for these patients 
should also be exercised when administering zolpidem due to the known 
risk of next-morning impairment. Additional agents for insomnia are listed 
in the Palliative Care Drug Appendix in the algorithm. 

Please also see the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain and the 
NCCN Guidelines for Cancer-Related Fatigue (available at 
www.NCCN.org) for their discussions on sleep/wake disturbances. 

Delirium 

The Panel emphasized the importance of maximizing nonpharmacologic 
interventions and considering risks and benefits in the context of prognosis 
for pharmacologic treatment of delirium.390 Limited studies are available to 
inform pharmacologic choices in treating delirium. A 2020 Cochrane 
review meta-analysis concluded that there was no high-quality evidence to 
support or recommend against drug therapy in patients with delirium at the 
end of life.391 Despite widespread use of antipsychotics for managing 
symptoms of delirium in palliative care, mixed evidence has been 
presented regarding use for delirium in patients with advanced cancer. In 
general, historical evidence supported the use of short-term, low-dose 

Delirium should be evaluated for severity and cause using the Diagnostic 
and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) 
criteria.384 NCCN DT for distress evaluation can be found in the NCCN 
Guidelines for Distress Management (available at www.NCCN.org). 
Potentially reversible causes should be identified and treated

antipsychotics for managing symptoms of delirium with close monitoring 
for potential adverse effects.392,393 Haloperidol has often been used as a 
first-line agent, with alternative options such as olanzapine, risperidone, 
and quetiapine, titrating dose to optimal effect with the lowest possible 
dose.394-396 However, current data favor the use of benzodiazepines over 
antipsychotics, particularly in mild to moderate delirium.397,398 In studies of 
patients receiving palliative care or critically ill patients in the ICU, 
antipsychotics such as haloperidol, risperidone, and ziprasidone were 
ineffective at significantly reducing symptoms of delirium.397,399 
Additionally, long-term follow-up did not confer any benefit. Additionally, in 
one trial, the cohort receiving placebo with supportive care had longer 
overall survival times than the cohort receiving haloperidol.397 Based on 
the mixed evidence available, the Panel recommends maximizing 
nonpharmacologic interventions and considering use of low-dose 
benzodiazepines with or without antipsychotic medications if agitation is 
severe and either disrupting care or causing the patient distress. 

are no longer necessary should be discontinued, and dose reductions of 
all other medications should be considered, especially if dependent on 
hepatic/renal function. Under- or overtreatment of pain can exacerbate 
delirium, as can fecal impaction, urinary tract infection (UTI), or distended 
bladder; these should be excluded as potential causes. Opioid rotation can 
be considered (see NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain [available at 
www.NCCN.org]) if the delirium is believed to be caused by neurotoxicity 
from the current opioid. If delirium is a result of disease progression and 
goals of care are comfort-oriented at the end of life, palliative care should 
be focused on symptom management and family support. Benzodiazepine 
medications with or without antipsychotics should be dose adjusted and/or 
have their route of administration changed to ensure adequate delirium 
symptom management, as appropriate.404 It is also important to note that 
sedation may be a side effect of the treatment, and it is recommended to 
ensure that the treatment plan is consistent with goals and prognosis. In 
severe delirium, sedation is also the goal and the evidence for effective 
pharmacologic intervention is conflicting and limited. It is also necessary to 
prepare the family and caregivers for delirium that may not resolve. For 
refractory delirium that is causing distress in dying patients, proportional 
sedation can be considered following consultation with a palliative care 
specialist and/or psychiatrist (see below). Please also see the NCCN 
Guidelines for Distress Management (available at www.NCCN.org) for 
further discussion of delirium in patients with cancer. 

Malignant Wounds 

The dosages of these symptom-management medications should be 
titrated to optimal effect with the lowest effective dose. Opioid dose 
reduction or rotation can also be considered for patients with severe 
delirium. In a recent multicenter, patient-based registry cohort study, Yoo 
et al400 found a significant, dose-dependent association between increased 
risk of delirium in patients with advanced cancer and use of opioid. 
Understanding the risks and benefits of treatments is important in shared 
decision-making. RT can be considered for patients with delirium due to 
brain metastases; however, there are currently no data demonstrating 
improvement, and palliative efforts should be intensified with the 
awareness that delirium is often a marker for a shorter prognosis.401-403 

Malignant wounds are the result of cancerous cells infiltrating the skin and 
its supporting blood and lymph vessels, causing loss in vascularity that 
leads to tissue death. Malignant wounds may originate as a primary 
cancer or as a metastasis to the skin from a local or distant tumor.405 
Malignant wounds may cause many distressing symptoms that negatively 
impact quality of life. In most cases, a combination of discharge, odor, 

For the dying patient, the focus should shift to family/caregiver support and 
education. Supportive caregivers should be allowed to be present at 
bedside if that aligns with patient and family preferences. Medications that

pages.text:
bleeding, pruritus, local inflammation, and/or pain accompany the wound, 
requiring medical attention and treatment.406 

(available at www.NCCN.org). For pruritus, topical doxepin cream, cooled 
hydrogel sheet dressings, and/or transcutaneous electrical nerve 
stimulation (TENS) trial are recommended. For body image, 
recommended strategies include maintaining symmetry in dressings, 
managing wound odor and exudate, screening for depression or anxiety, 
and addressing intimacy concerns. 

Social Support/Resource Management 

For distress related to psychological or psychiatric complications and 
spiritual or existential crisis, please see the NCCN Guidelines for Distress 
Management (available at www.NCCN.org). 

The Panel recommends treating malignant wounds if potentially reversible 
in patients with an estimated life expectancy of months to years. 
Management of malignant wounds may include treatment of underlying 
cancer and comorbid conditions, including poor nutritional status that 
increases risk for impaired wound healing; local wound management; and 
symptom relief. Treatment options include surgical debridement, skin 
grafting, wound-directed treatment with radiation, systemic treatment, 
vacuum-assisted wound closure, wound cleansing/irrigation, dressing 
changes, treating infection, optimizing nutrition/mobilization, and 
preventing wound spread. Cancer-directed systemic therapy may need to 
be adjusted based on associated side effects of antineoplastic drugs and 
risk to exacerbate wounds.406 Selection of the appropriate wound 
dressing is highly important for malignant wound care and, if available, 
the Panel recommends consultation with wound care specialists. 

For best outcomes, psychosocial-spiritual support should be integrated 
into routine cancer care across all disease stages and in both the inpatient 
and outpatient settings.30,407-409 A systematic review of patients with 
advanced cancer identified psychosocial-spiritual resources among the 
factors that promoted personal growth during the experience of cancer.410 

In the dying patient, the Panel recommends interventions focused on 
symptom relief. For odor, wound cleansing/debridement, topical antibiotic 
gel, activated charcoal/silver sulfadiazine dressings, external odor 
absorbers, and/or avoiding strong “cover” odors are recommended. For 
infection, topical/systemic antibiotics and/or irradiated honey applications 
are recommended. For exudate, absorbent alginate, foam dressings, 
and/or drainage stoma appliance (if high volume) are recommended. For 
bleeding, hemostatic dressings (alginate, collagen, non-adherent gauze, 
gelfoam, and sucralfate paste), oral antifibrinolytics, radiotherapy or 
embolization (if brisk bleeding), dark-colored linens, anxiolytics, and/or 
pain management are recommended. For pain, use of non-absorbent 
dressing or reducing frequency of dressing changes may be considered. 
Topical opioid and/or local anesthetic may be applied. Pain should be 
treated according to the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain 

For patients with estimated life expectancy ranging from months to years 
experiencing psychosocial-spiritual distress, social support/resource 
management should be offered. Patient/family/caregiver(s)’ coping and 
adjustment to the illness should be assessed, along with the safety of the 
environment and the availability of caregivers. In addition, it is important to 
ensure that the patient has adequate access to transportation and 
sufficient financial resources. Assessment for substance use disorders 
may be done according to the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain 
(available at www.NCCN.org). Cultural issues, including the need for 
medical interpreters/translators unrelated to the patient, should be 
addressed. Support from social services (social worker, psychologist, 
and/or psychiatrist) may also be appropriate for the patient as well as 
caregivers and family members, and should be provided in the form of 
counseling, child life services, art and music therapy (if available), support

management; 3) reduction of patient/family/caregiver distress; 4) 
acceptable sense of control; 5) decision-making capacity; 6) decreased 
caregiver burden; 7) strengthened relationships; 8) optimized quality of 
life; 9) personal growth and enhanced meaning; and 10) advanced care 
planning in progress.415-418 

groups, and physical medicine/rehabilitation training for transfers and 
repositioning.411-413 Personal, spiritual, or cultural issues related to the 
patient’s illness and prognosis should be addressed.414 Family/caregivers 
need to be periodically assessed and monitored for risk factors associated 
with complicated grief. Respite care for families and caregivers in crisis 
should be considered. Complexities related to social determinants of 
health need to be assessed and addressed adequately according to the 
NCCN DT and Problem List as part of the NCCN Guidelines for Distress 
Management (available at www.NCCN.org). 

If there are ongoing needs, upon reassessment, the oncology or palliative 
care team should reevaluate intervention options and intensify as possible, 
if needed. The Panel also recommends promoting adaptive coping 
strategies.419 The oncology team should also consult specialized palliative 
care services, hospice, or an ethics committee when needed. Consultation 
with a mental health professional and/or addiction specialist to evaluate 
and treat undiagnosed psychiatric disorders and substance use disorders 
should be considered as appropriate. If psychosocial-spiritual distress 
persists, palliative care options should be intensified, and patients should 
receive care according to the NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management 
(available at www.NCCN.org). 

Patients’ treatment goals and expectations may change and evolve as 
disease progresses. Reassessment should be ongoing, with continuation 
or modification of life-expectancy–guided palliative care until the patient’s 
death or survivorship. 

In a dying patient with an estimated life expectancy of days to weeks, the 
patient’s desires for comfort should be evaluated and supported. The 
process of dying and the expected events should be explained to the 
patient, family, and caregivers. Child life services should be provided if 
appropriate and available, and clinicians should respond to caregiver-
specific demands, stresses, and conflicts (consider social work referral). 
Medical interpreters/translators who are not related to the patient and 
family may be obtained as needed. Periodic reassessment and monitoring 
of family/caregiver(s) for risk factors associated with complicated grief is 
recommended. Culturally and spiritually congruent care should be 
ensured. Eligibility, readiness, and need for specialized palliative/hospice 
care including open access hospice programs (if available) should be 
determined. 

End-of-Life Care Issues 

Palliative Care Reassessment 

Preparing Patients/Families/Caregivers for End-of-Life and 
Transition to Hospice Care 

A multicenter survey of acute care hospitals revealed discordance 
between patients’ stated values and corresponding treatment preferences 
for end-of-life care. The study highlighted the need for medical decision 
support to ensure that patient preferences were grounded in a clear 
understanding of their illness and end-of-life treatment options.420 SPC 
consultation should be considered to assist in conflict resolution when the 

All patients should be reassessed regularly, and effective communication 
and information sharing must exist between the patient, caregivers, and 
health care providers. Patients and family members benefit most from 
ongoing discussions about the natural history of the disease and 
prognosis in clear, consistent language. Desired outcomes as a result of 
palliative care assessment and intervention include the following: 1) 
patient satisfied with response to cancer therapy; 2) adequate symptom 

MS-29

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
patient, family, and/or medical professional team do not agree on the 
benefit/efficacy of interventions. 

Dying patients may wish to prepare for death and help prepare family 
members to go on without them. Both patients and families benefit from 
education in the dying process. Families and caregivers should be guided 
through their anticipatory grief, and arrangements should be made to 
ensure that the patient, family, and caregiver needs and goals regarding 
the dying process are respected. Planning to ensure continuing care and 
referrals to appropriate care is important. Arrangements should be 
available to ensure that the patient does not die alone unless that is the 
patient’s preference. Other involved health care professionals should be 
informed of the patient’s death. 

Response to Expressions of Distress Including Request for 
Hastened Death 

For patients with an estimated life expectancy of years or months to years, 
health care professionals should engage in clear, consistent discussion 
with the patient, family, and caregiver(s) about prognosis and anticipated 
care needs on an ongoing basis. Advance care planning should be 
initiated, along with an assessment of decision-making capacity and the 
need to identify a surrogate decision-maker. Providers should elicit patient 
values and preferences with respect to quality of life and the need for 
specialized palliative care, or eligibility and readiness for hospice care 
should be introduced, educated, and assessed as appropriate. When the 
patient’s functional status indicates a 6- to 12-month prognosis, a 
dedicated “hospice information” visit with the oncologist may ease 
transition to hospice care in the future by preparing the patient, family, and 
caregiver(s), and reassuring them that their oncologist can remain 
involved. 

For patients with an estimated life expectancy of weeks to months or days 
to weeks, the oncology team should assess patient/family/caregiver 
understanding of the dying process and provide education as needed. 
Providers should address potential need for transitions in care while 
ensuring continued involvement of the primary care physician and primary 
oncology team. Referrals should be made to hospice care agencies, as 
well as for psychosocial assessment, grief counseling, spiritual screening, 
and funeral/memorial service planning, as necessary. The goals and 
needs of the patient and family regarding the dying process should be 
respected. Legacy work may be explored during assessment for the 
patient since such activities are simple to implement, can reduce caregiver 
stress, and can improve the peace and dignity of the patient since they will 
be able to contribute to how they will be remembered, which tends to be 
beneficial to all involved.421-423 

The most appropriate initial response to an expression of distress 
including a request for hastened death is to explore the meanings behind 
that request and ensure palliative care needs are being met.424 The 
AAHPM has released a position statement and advisory brief regarding 
this topic with guidance for health care professionals on how to evaluate 
and respond to these requests.425,426 The Panel recommends that patients 
expressing distress such as requesting hastened death may be referred to 
their SPC team. Open exploration of the patient’s expression of distress 
including a request for hastened death may identify unmet needs and new 
palliative care interventions that may be helpful.424,427 Concerns related to 
the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, voluntary cessation of eating 
and drinking, and/or sedation should be discussed with patients and 
families. Psychiatric consultation to evaluate and treat reversible causes of 
psychological suffering should be considered. Patients should be assured 
that their health care team is committed to providing continuing care. It is 
important for physicians to know the local legal status and local health 
system policies and procedures of medical aid in dying (MAID), as other 
states have pending legislation regarding either prohibiting or permitting 
MAID.424 Several organizations have released position statements and/or

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
helpful websites on the issue of MAID (see Table 1 at the end of this 
Discussion section). 

Shared Decision-Making in the Care of the Imminently Dying Patient 

symptoms of dying and the rationale for discontinuation of treatment or 
medications that may not add to the patient’s comfort. The care plan may 
also include consultation with the SPC team to meet the social and 
spiritual needs of the patient and their family/caregivers; counseling to 
promote healthy grieving; support for children/grandchildren; and 
education for parents on age-appropriate grieving processes. Anticipatory 
bereavement support should be offered along with an assessment for 
complicated bereavement risk. 431,432 

An imminently dying patient is defined as one within hours of death who is 
not stable enough for transport.428 Caring for an imminently dying patient is 
intense for the patient, family, caregiver(s), and health care team. An 
international qualitative study described many of the common 
non-pharmacologic palliative care activities provided in the last days of 
life.429 An end-of-life care order set for patients wishing to focus on comfort 
that includes physical, practical, and psychosocial-spiritual interventions 
may be beneficial for practitioners to use for imminently dying patients. If 
not already done, obtaining a hospice evaluation may also be helpful. 

For patients whose goals shift to comfort at the end of life, the physical 
aspects of care for an imminently dying patient focus on adequate 
symptom management. Approaches may include intensifying comfort 
care; discontinuation of unnecessary diagnostic tests and interventions; 
deactivation of implanted devices as indicated; alternate routes of 
medication administration if the oral route is not feasible; and managing 
terminal secretions, delirium, and dyspnea. Proportional sedation can be 
considered for refractory symptoms.251,263,430 It is also important to be 
prepared for patient and family requests for autopsy and/or organ 
donation. 

The practical aspects of care for an imminently dying patient in the 
hospital include mobilizing in-hospital end-of-life care policy and 
procedures; ensuring that the patient’s advance directive is documented 
and implemented; securing a private room for the patient when possible; 
and enabling family presence around the clock as appropriate. If not 
already done, patient/family/caregiver wishes for resuscitation should be 
discussed and documented. In this context, CPR is unlikely to be effective; 
providers should recommend other options for resuscitation such as “Do 
Not Resuscitate” (DNR), “Do Not Attempt Resuscitation” (DNAR), and 
“Allow Natural Death” (AND) orders and promote comfort care. Providers 
should be aware that policies regarding resuscitation may differ based on 
treatment setting. A patient with a documented inpatient DNAR order may 
also require DNAR orders for out-of-hospital settings (eg, residential care, 
ambulance transport). In states where MOLST/POLST has been 
established, it is important to complete this document, as it will protect the 
patient’s wishes across all treatment settings. If in-person visits are 
restricted or not possible, facilitate virtual visits. 

Proportional Sedation 

The psychosocial-spiritual aspects of care for an imminently dying patient 
whose goals have transitioned to comfort focus on individual and family 
goals, preferences, cultures, and religious beliefs. Open communication 
should occur between the patient, family, caregiver(s), and care team 
regarding the physical and psychological aspects of the dying process and 
the importance of honoring any advance directives. The 
patient/family/caregiver(s) should be educated about the signs and 

Proportional sedation (PS; formerly known as palliative sedation) is the 
intentional lowering of awareness towards, and including, 
unconsciousness for patients with severe and refractory symptoms with 
the primary goal of symptom relief. The NCCN Guidelines committee has 

MS-31

pages.title: Palliative Care
pages.text:
of necessary paperwork; and informing insurance companies and previous 
medical, palliative, and psychological care teams of the patient’s death. 

replaced the term palliative sedation with proportional sedation. The 
change is intended to emphasize that the level of sedation should be 
proportionate to the patient’s symptom burden. PS may be considered for 
imminently dying patients (life expectancy of hours to days) with refractory 
symptoms that persist despite comprehensive, interprofessional palliative 
care.433,434 The Panel recommends referring to institutional 
guidelines/policy and state/national regulations for additional guidance, as 
well as involvement of an ethics consultation as appropriate.434 

Generally, if PS is being considered, a prognosis of imminent death should 
be confirmed and informed consent must be obtained from the patient 
and/or a surrogate or family member following discussions of the patient’s 
disease status, treatment goals, prognosis, and expected outcomes.435 

Bereavement support should be offered, beginning with a personal visit or 
telephone call from the patient’s primary oncology team, followed by a 
condolence letter. Periodic assessment and monitoring of 
family/caregiver(s) for risk factors associated with complicated grief is 
recommended. Persistent complex bereavement disorder is a condition 
characterized by intense, prolonged symptoms of grief, coupled with 
functional impairment beyond 6 months post-loss.431,444-446 Children of 
patients with cancer represent a uniquely at-risk population for 
psychosocial dysfunction. Additionally, a study suggested that certain 
predictors of prolonged grief could be identified in family caregivers at the 
time of the patient’s entry to palliative care; these factors include severity 
of pre-death symptoms; condition of the caregiver’s relationship to the 
patient; impact of caregiving duties on the caregiver’s schedule; quality of 
family functioning; and level of optimism, especially if low.447 

PS has its ethical justification in the Doctrine of Double Effect,436-441 which 
provides guidance for situations where an attempt to do good may have 
unwanted side effects (eg, providing medication for the relief of suffering 
that also causes sedation). Studies have investigated whether palliative 
sedation shortens survival. Results obtained from systematic reviews did 
not reveal a clear impact of palliative sedation on survival time, although 
many of the included studies lacked high-quality data.442,443 

After-Death Care Interventions 

Bereavement care is often best provided by an experienced hospice team 
or a skilled mental health care professional. The family may request a 
debriefing meeting from the medical team and may require assistance in 
identifying community bereavement resources. A well-supported 
end-of-life care experience will facilitate the family’s acceptance of 
appropriate referrals for cancer risk assessment and risk modification. If 
not already recommended, providers should direct family members 
towards genetic screening, especially if the deceased patient was positive 
for known genetic markers that confer risk. For more information, see the 
NCCN Guidelines for Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Breast, 
Ovarian, Pancreatic, and Prostate and NCCN Guidelines for 
Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Colorectal, Endometrial, 
Esophageal, and Gastric (available at www.NCCN.org). 

Comprehensive palliative care for the patient’s family and caregivers 
continues after the patient’s death. Immediate issues include informing the 
family (if not present), offering condolences, and providing the family time 
with the body. Spiritual care provider involvement to assess the family's 
desire for religious ritual or spiritual support may be helpful. Additional 
concerns include ensuring culturally sensitive and respectful treatment of 
the body, including removal of tubes, drains, lines, and the Foley catheter 
(unless an autopsy is planned); addressing concerns about organ 
donation or autopsy; facilitating funeral arrangements through completion
