Putting Palliative Care Guidelines into Practice 

Institutions should develop processes for integrating palliative care into 
cancer care, both as part of usual oncology care and for patients with SPC 
needs. Many approaches to this have been described, but there is no 
single best practice.21-29,448 

team allows patients to meet the individuals who will help them and their 
families through their experience. Because the diagnosis of cancer and 
impending death is such a frightening experience, oncologists must work 
to alleviate those fears by assuring patients that the members of the 
oncology and palliative care teams will work with them and their families 
regardless of what happens. Additionally, oncologists must discuss 
prognosis with both the family and the palliative care team in order to 
anticipate and manage concerns commonly associated with the diagnosis 
and treatment of cancer. 

Patients and families should be informed that palliative care is an integral 
part of their comprehensive cancer care. Educational programs should be 
provided to all health care professionals and trainees so that they can 
develop effective palliative care knowledge, skills, and perspectives. 
Skilled palliative care specialists and interprofessional palliative care 
teams, including board-certified palliative care physicians and advanced 
practice providers, should be readily available to provide consultative or 
direct care to patients and families who request or require their expertise. 
Finally, the quality of palliative care should be monitored by institutional 
quality improvement programs. 

As the disease progresses, many patients and families need help coping 
with the implications of increasing disease burden. Some patients and 
families have great difficulty accepting a poor prognosis and, as a result, 
do not engage in advance care planning.449,450 This may be a sign of 
imperfect understanding of the disease and should be addressed directly 
and compassionately.450 Palliative care supports ongoing education to 
help patients and families better understand and prepare for disease 
progression. 

The experiences of patients with cancer begin with diagnosis, and many 
palliative care questions should be considered early in the comprehensive 
cancer care plan. As cancer progresses and the value of further 
anticancer therapy diminishes, palliative measures should be intensified. 
Clear and consistent discussion of goals, values, preferences, prognostic 
information, and therapeutic options can help patients, families, and 
providers make appropriate decisions in a shared manner. 

Oncologists should encourage advance care planning early in the disease 
trajectory in order to assess and cultivate prognostic awareness and 
create a care plan that is consistent with the patient’s wishes. In addition, 
advance care planning can lessen the burden of making difficult end-of-life 
decisions. The combined efforts of the oncology team and the 
hospice/palliative care team can improve the overall outcome for patients 
and their families. 

Psychosocial, Spiritual, and Existential Support for 
Oncology and Palliative Care Providers 

After the loss of a patient, psychosocial-spiritual support should be 
available for providers who have been involved in the patient’s care. A 
bereavement or memorial ritual, such as a brief reading or moment of 

Undergoing anticancer therapy should not preclude addressing end-of-life 
issues. Collaborating with palliative care experts on such matters extends 
oncologists’ therapeutic repertoire and diminishes the stress of caring for 
patients who have incurable disease. Increasing emphasis on palliative 
care in oncology should improve patient outcomes and provide new 
avenues for clinical research and professional satisfaction. The timely 
introduction of members of the institutional or community palliative care

quiet, can be considered. Funeral attendance by health care professionals 
may also be considered. Health care professionals should review medical 
issues related to patient death, explore concerns and questions about 
quality of patient care, and review emotional responses of family and staff 
to the patient’s death. 

demonstrated that mindfulness training through the Stress Management 
and Resiliency Training (SMART) program was able to improve anxiety, 
stress, quality of life, and mindfulness among providers.461-463 A 
meta-analysis of efficacy data on meditative interventions for health 
professionals demonstrated a small to moderate benefit according to 
measures of emotional exhaustion (effect size 0.37; 95% CI, 0.04–0.70), 
sense of personal accomplishment (effect size 1.18; 95% CI, 0.10–2.25), 
and life satisfaction (effect size 0.48; 95% CI, 0.15–0.81).464 

Qualitative research on compassion fatigue interventions reveals that 
oncology clinicians rated the following resources as helpful: educational 
interventions, support programs or resources in the workplace, retreats, 
and self-care measures.451,465 Unfortunately, despite the reported desire 
for such interventions, access can be limited. In a nationwide survey of 
oncology nurses, only 60% of survey respondents reported access to an 
employee assistance program, 45% reported no offerings of education 
addressing workplace coping, and 82% of respondents reported no off-site 
programs such as retreats.465 

Oncology and palliative care teams commonly encounter patient loss and 
deal with grief, and over time the resultant emotional distress can lead to 
compromised resilience, including provider burnout, intra-team conflicts or 
disagreements, compassion fatigue, and ethical concerns or moral 
distress.451-455 These syndromes can manifest as symptoms of depression, 
anxiety, fatigue, and low mental quality of life.456 Personnel experiencing 
such symptoms should be identified and assisted. Considerable research 
has been dedicated to evaluating patterns of patient, family, and caregiver 
grief, and interventions to mediate this distress. Far less attention has 
been devoted to similar issues among health care providers and teams; 
further research is needed. For a summary of the literature on compassion 
fatigue and burnout among oncology providers, see reviews by Najjar and 
colleagues,451 Shanafelt and Dyrbye,456 and Sherman and colleagues.457 

Generally, evidence-based interventions for compassion fatigue, moral 
distress, and burnout in physicians are lacking. When asked to provide 
useful preventive measures and coping strategies, palliative care 
specialists recommended emphasizing the rewarding aspects of their work 
and strategies for “enhanced meaning-making.”466 Experts in the field have 
also highlighted the importance of self-awareness and self-care measures 
for oncologists and palliative care specialists to decrease levels of 
compassion fatigue.467 To this end, self-care was established as a core 
competency area for fellows in hospice and palliative medicine.467 
Examples and evidence for additional preventive strategies and solutions 
for oncologist burnout have been reviewed by Shanafelt and Dyrbye.456 

Although limited in quantity, most studies on compassion fatigue are 
derived from the oncology nursing literature. A large survey of hospice and 
palliative care providers (eg, clinical, administrative, allied health workers) 
revealed a strong correlation between burnout and compassion fatigue, 
and revealed the need for enhanced support of individuals in this field.458 
Additionally, a cross-sectional survey of nurses, medical assistants, and 
radiology technicians at a comprehensive cancer center revealed 
concerning levels of burnout and compassion fatigue in both inpatient and 
outpatient care settings.459 A resiliency program was piloted and 
eventually scaled hospital-wide to educate providers on these issues and 
provide interventional strategies. Improvements in burnout and secondary 
traumatic stress were observed.459,460 Several studies from the Mayo Clinic

pages.text:
Conclusion 

These Guidelines are intended to help oncology teams incorporate 
palliative care into their practice and thereby provide the best and most 
comprehensive cancer treatment possible for patients with incurable 
cancer. Patients with advanced disease may be overly optimistic about 
their chances of cure and survival, and this can have a negative effect on 
their quality of life. One study found that those who overestimated their 
survival were more likely to die a bad death.121 Using a decision aid, Smith 
et al found that most patients want honest information, even if it is bad 
news.468 Although use of the decision aid typically took 20 minutes and 
was challenging for oncologists, it did not cause patients to give up hope 
or become distressed. Physician-led discussion of disease progression 
and death can improve quality of care and quality of life for both patients 
and families.469 Providing information in a collaborative manner protects 
the autonomy of patients to make informed decisions based on potential 
treatment outcomes.470 Palliative care can help patients and families set 
realistic expectations and meet short- and longer-term goals, such as 
important life-cycle events. Much of the care outlined in these Guidelines 
is geared toward a different hope than that for cure of the disease 
itself.132,468,471 Even when cure is no longer possible, hope remains: hope 
for dignity, comfort, and closure and for growth at the end of life. It is our 
hope that these Guidelines will help oncology and palliative care 
professionals together create a better future for patients, families, and 
providers.

nodes.text: Palliative care is an approach to patient-/family-/caregiver-centered health care that focuses on optimal management of distressing symptoms, while incorporating psychosocial, spiritual support according to patient/family/caregiver needs, values, beliefs, and cultures. Unless otherwise stated, these guidelines encourage the involvement of each patient’s support network, as determined by the patient and abbreviated here as patient/family/caregiver, in all aspects of care as needed and appropriate. The goal of palliative care is to anticipate, prevent, and reduce suffering; promote adaptive coping; and support the best possible quality of life for patients/families/caregivers, regardless of the stage of the disease or the need for other therapies. Palliative care can begin at diagnosis; be delivered concurrently with disease-directed, life-prolonging therapies; and facilitate patient autonomy, access to information, and choice. Palliative care only becomes the main focus of care when disease-directed, life-prolonging therapies are no longer effective, appropriate, or desired.

nodes.text: Standards of Palliative Care • Palliative care should be provided by the primary oncology team and augmented as needed by collaboration with an interprofessional team of palliative care experts including but not limited to board-certified palliative care physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses, social workers, spiritual care providers, mental health professionals, and pharmacists. These team members are referred to as “specialty palliative care team” throughout the guideline and should be available to provide consultative or direct care to patients/families/caregivers and/or health care professionals who request or require their expertise. • Institutions should develop processes for integrating palliative care into cancer care, both as part of usual oncology care and for patients with specialty palliative care needs. • All patients with cancershould be screened for palliative care needs at their initial visit, at appropriate intervals, and as clinically indicated (see PAL-2 and PAL-3). • Patients/families/caregivers should be informed that palliative care is an integral part of their comprehensive cancer care. • Educational programs should be provided to all health care professionals and trainees so that they can develop effective palliative care knowledge, skills, and attitudes. • Quality of palliative care should be monitored by institutional quality improvement programs.

nodes.text: We believe that expressions of distress (including wishing not to live in one's current state or wishing for a hastened death) often have important meanings that merit exploration. The most appropriate initial response to expressions of distress is to ensure palliative care needs are being met. Patients making such a request may be referred to a specialty palliative care team. However, evaluating expressions of distress (including a patient's request for hastened death) is an important skill, even for clinicians who feel medical aid in dying (MAID) is never morally acceptable. Clarifying these meanings may enlarge the range of useful therapeutic options and might reduce the patient's wish to die.

nodes.text: Explore the reasons for expressions of distress (including a request for hastened death), and find out "why now" in a joint discussion with the patient, family, and caregivers. • Reassess concerns and/or symptom management. • Assess patient concerns regarding symptoms. • Reassess psychological/psychiatric issues, especially depression, anxiety, grief, psychosis, delirium, and dementia. • Ask about the patient's relationship to family or other important people. • Ask about individual values, purpose and meaning, and personal views of spiritual/existential suffering and consider spiritual care consultation for further exploration and intervention. • Assess for worries about caregiver burden and abandonment and re-emphasize physician commitment to the patient.

nodes.text: Examine your own response as a clinician to a particular patient's request. Expressions of distress (including requests for hastened death) can force clinicians to confront their own personal, professional, moral, and legal responsibilities. Dealing with an individual patient can be quite different from thinking about the issue in abstract circumstances. Consider a consultation with an ethics committee, palliative care service, or experienced colleague. These cases are usually complex and often benefit from consideration of multiple perspectives.

nodes.text: Obtain hospice evaluation, if available • Intensify comfort measures ◊Implement skin safety protocol according to risk assessment: – Regularly reposition the patient for comfort as indicated – Reassess and premedicate for wound care as needed – Use a pressure-relieving mattress, if available – Provide eye and mouth care to maintain moisture – Treat for urinary retention and fecal impaction • Ensure deactivation of implanted defibrillator • Consider deactivation of implanted pacemaker in select patients • Discontinue unnecessary diagnostic tests and interventions such as transfusions, needle sticks, blood glucose monitoring, oxygen saturation monitoring, and suctioning • Replace check of vital signs with regular (eg, every 4 h) symptom assessments • Switch routes of medication administration when the oral route is no longer feasible • Adjust doses of medications to optimal comfort • Treat terminal secretions (death rattle): ◊Educate patient and caregiver ◊Reduce parenteral and enteral fluids ◊Reposition the patient ◊Provide gentle oropharyngeal suctioning (avoid deep suctioning) ◊Utilize nonpharmacologic interventions first before anti- secretory agents • Treat dyspnea by adjusting the dose of medication (PAL-11) • Treat delirium PAL-24. See NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management • Consider proportional sedation for refractory symptoms (PAL-33) • Be prepared to discuss a request for organ donation and autopsy

nodes.text: • Proportional sedation (formerly known as palliative sedation) is the intentional lowering of awareness towards, and including, unconsciousness for patients with severe and refractory symptoms with the primary goal of symptom relief. • Refractory symptoms are symptoms that cannot be adequately managed despite comprehensive, interprofessional palliative care that does not compromise consciousness. • Consider interdisciplinary discussion prior to inception of sedation and throughout the process, to support the care team (including both the caregivers and family in support of the patient, and the medical staff taking care of the patient). • Consider periodic reassessment of symptoms to ensure level of sedation is proportional to need for symptom relief. • Refer to institutional guidelines/policy for additional guidance. • "A patient who is suffering from a terminal illness and who is experiencing great pain has no legal barriers to obtaining medication, from qualified physicians, to alleviate suffering, even to the point of unconsciousness and hastening death.” -Justice O’Connor (see Vacco v Quill and Washington v Glucksberg, 1997). • The NCCN Guidelines committee has replaced the term palliative sedation with proportional sedation. The change is intended to emphasize that the level of sedation should be proportionate to the patient’s symptom burden.

prognosis_window.criteria: Years; Months to year; Weeks to months; Days to weeks (dying patient)
prognosis_window.definition: Clinician-estimated time-to-death window for the patient, as stated in the case.

diarrhea_stool_increase_per_day.definition: Increase in stools per day over the patient's baseline (ostomy output not counted here).

symptom_pain.definition: Patient has pain as an active symptom.

symptom_dyspnea.definition: Patient has dyspnea as an active symptom.

symptom_fatigue_weakness_asthenia.definition: Patient has fatigue, weakness or asthenia.

symptom_insomnia_sedation.definition: Patient has insomnia or sedation problems.

symptom_distress.definition: Patient has psychological distress as a symptom.

symptom_fertility_intimacy.definition: Patient has fertility or intimacy concerns.

symptom_oral_care.definition: Patient has an oral care problem.

existential_psychosocial_spiritual_distr.definition: Patient has existential, psychosocial or spiritual distress or spiritual/existential needs.

educational_informational_needs.definition: Patient, family or caregivers have educational or informational needs.

complex_patient_family_circumstances.definition: Complex patient, family or caregiver circumstances are present.

oncology_team_staff_challenges.definition: Challenges within the oncology care team or staff are present.

social_practical_challenges.definition: Social or practical challenges or concerns are present.

distress_thermometer_score.definition: Score on the standardized distress screening instrument (distress thermometer, 0-10) as recorded in the case.

distress_classification_stated.definition: Whether the case explicitly states a high or not-high level of psychological distress on standardized screening. not_stated if the case does not state it.

pain_nrs_score.definition: Current pain intensity on the numeric rating scale (0-10) as recorded in the case.

pain_conventional_interventions_failed_c.definition: Number of conventional pain interventions that have been tried without adequate relief.

pain_management_risk_stated.definition: Whether the case explicitly states high risk of poor pain management, or pain resistant to conventional interventions. not_stated if the case does not state it.

limited_cancer_treatment_options.definition: Cancer treatment options are limited (limited access, or disease refractory to cancer treatment).

limited_access_to_cancer_treatment.definition: Limited access to cancer treatment is present (one finding of limited cancer treatment options).

disease_refractory_to_cancer_treatment.definition: Disease is refractory to cancer treatment (one finding of limited cancer treatment options).

ongoing_needs_present.definition: Clinician judgement after reassessment that the patient still has ongoing palliative needs.

nv_etiology_chemo_rt_induced.definition: Nausea/vomiting attributed to chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

nv_etiology_cns_involvement.definition: Nausea/vomiting attributed to central nervous system involvement.

nv_etiology_gi_obstruction_or_liver_meta.definition: Nausea/vomiting attributed to gastrointestinal obstruction from intra-abdominal tumor or liver metastasis.

nv_etiology_gastritis_or_gerd.definition: Nausea/vomiting attributed to gastritis or gastroesophageal reflux disease.

nv_etiology_dehydration_uremia_hypercalc.definition: Nausea/vomiting attributed to another cause such as dehydration, uremia or hypercalcemia.

nv_etiology_medication_or_substance.definition: Nausea/vomiting attributed to medication or substance use.

nv_etiology_non_specific.definition: Nausea/vomiting without an identified specific cause.

dyspnea_unrelieved_on_treatment.definition: Dyspnea remains unrelieved despite current treatment.

patient_desires_insomnia_sedation_treatm.definition: Patient wants insomnia or sedation treated.

poor_surgery_ascites.definition: Ascites is present (risk factor for poor surgical outcome).

poor_surgery_carcinomatosis.definition: Carcinomatosis is present (risk factor for poor surgical outcome).

palpable_intra_abdominal_mass.definition: A palpable intra-abdominal mass is present (risk factor for poor surgical outcome).

multifocal_bowel_obstruction.definition: Bowel obstructions are multifocal (risk factor for poor surgical outcome).

previous_abdominal_radiation.definition: Patient has had previous abdominal radiation (risk factor for poor surgical outcome).

surgical_candidate_judgement.definition: Clinician judgement that the patient is a candidate for operative management (resection, bypass or diverting ostomy).

advance_care_planning_documents_complete.definition: Patient has completed advance care planning documents.

goals_transitioned_to_comfort.definition: Patient's goals of care have transitioned to comfort.

high_psychological_distress_screen.criteria_source: external: NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management (distress thermometer score of 4 or higher)
high_psychological_distress_screen.definition: High level of psychological distress based on standardized distress screening. The box names the NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management, so the standard definition is used: distress thermometer score of 4 or higher (0-10 scale). A case that explicitly states the classification uses the stated value instead of the score.

pain_high_risk_poor_management_or_refrac.definition: High risk of poor pain management, or pain that remains resistant to conventional interventions. The box prints this criterion as 'High risk of poor pain management or pain that remains resistant to conventional interventions'; the quantitative criteria are in NCCN Adult Cancer Pain (PAIN-K, PAIN-L, PAIN-M), which the box references but does not reproduce, so the classification follows the case statement; the raw pain measures are stored for later rules.

diarrhea_grade.definition: Diarrhea grade from the stool increase over baseline. Thresholds are as printed in the boxes (Mild/Grade 1: increase of <4 stools/day; Moderate/Grade 2: increase of 4-6; Severe/Grade 3: increase of >7); an exact value of 7 stools is not covered by the printed thresholds and is returned as unclassified.

delirium_severity.definition: Delirium severity. Severe means delirium with agitation (printed as 'Severe delirium (agitation)'); mild/moderate is delirium without agitation (printed as 'Mild/ moderate delirium').

limited_cancer_treatment_options_from_fi.definition: Limited cancer treatment options due to limited access to cancer treatment, or disease refractory to cancer treatment (printed as 'Limited cancer treatment options due to: Limited access to cancer treatment; Disease refractory to cancer treatment'). True if any listed finding is present.

specialty_pc_consult_indicated.definition: Criteria for consideration of consultation with the specialty palliative care team are met (printed as high psychological distress, high risk of poor pain management or refractory pain, or limited cancer treatment options).

poor_surgical_outcome_risk.definition: At least one listed risk factor for poor surgical outcome is present (printed as ascites, carcinomatosis, palpable intra-abdominal masses, multifocal bowel obstructions, previous abdominal radiation).

shared_decision_making_imminent_dying.definition: Patient is in the days-to-weeks dying window and goals have transitioned to comfort (printed as 'For an imminently dying patient whose goals have transitioned to comfort').

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
